VIDEO.title: The Lesson Everyone MISSED At Jesus' Arrest
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 26:30-46 · Episode 52 (#55 of 58 in the playlist)
hand: Where the flesh fails, prayer succeeds
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 26:30-46. After the hymn they go to the Mount of Olives. Jesus says they will all fall away, quoting 'I will strike down the shepherd,' but after He is raised He will go ahead of them to Galilee. Peter insists he will never fall away and will die with Jesus; all the disciples say the same. In Gethsemane Jesus takes Peter, James and John, says His soul is deeply grieved to the point of death, and prays three times, 'let this cup pass from Me; yet not as I will, but as You will.' Three times He finds them sleeping.

Mark, Luke and John record these events slightly differently. 'You will all fall away' uses skandalizō, the word of Jesus' warning in 11:6. Jesus says 'I have been raised' (26:32), though elsewhere He says He will raise up the sanctuary of His body (John 2:19-21).

Gethsemane means 'oil press.' Jesus separates to be alone with the Father. His human inclination to avoid the cup of wrath gives way at once to the Father's will. Jesus shows the spirit's victory over the flesh; the disciples, who had just vowed to die for Him, show the flesh's victory over the spirit.

Connections: Zechariah 13:7 ('Strike the Shepherd'); the refrains of Psalms 42-43 ('Why are you in despair, O my soul?'), which end in joy at the altar of God (43:4); the Passover 'night to be kept' (Exodus 12:42); the cup of wrath (Isaiah 51:17; Ezekiel 23:33). Jesus' prayer echoes the Lord's Prayer (6:9-13): Father, Your will be done, deliver us, do not lead us into temptation.

The lesson: the victory of the Christian in moments of testing and temptation trades on persistent, intentional prayer to their heavenly Father. Peter and Paul passed it on (1 Peter 5:8-9; Ephesians 6:18; 1 Corinthians 10:12-13).
QUOTES: The victory of the Christian in moments of testing and temptation trades on persistent intentional prayer to their heavenly father.
The disciples are displaying what it looks like for the flesh to have victory over the spirit.
The flesh will fail in moments of testing and temptation. But where the flesh fails, prayer succeeds.
Jesus shows the disciples that the way of escape centers on diligent prayer.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Keep watching and praying that you may not enter into temptation; the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.
My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; yet not as I will, but as You will.

No temptation has overtaken you but such as is common to man, but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will provide the way of escape also, so that you will be able to endure it.

left.text: Then Jesus *said to them, “You will all fall away because of Me this night, for it is written, ‘I will strike down the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.’

right.text: “Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd / And against the man, My Associate,” / Declares Yahweh of hosts. / “Strike the Shepherd that the sheep may be scattered; / And I will turn My hand against the little ones.

lines.text: 'Fall away' is a form of skandalizō, the word of Jesus' warning to John's disciples: 'blessed is he who does not take offense at Me' (11:6). The disciples will do the very thing He warned against.
Jesus speaks of 'after I have been raised' (26:32); in John He says He will raise up the sanctuary of His body (John 2:19-21; 10:18). Both descriptions of the resurrection stand.

src.text: Jesus said to him, “Truly I say to you that this very night, before a rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.” Peter *said to Him, “Even if I have to die with You, I will not deny You.” All the disciples said the same thing too.

lines.text: The disciples say nothing about His death and resurrection; only Peter answers, bothered by the claim that they will fall away. And it is not just Peter: all of them say they are ready to die. Or so they thought.

src.text: Then Jesus *came with them to a place called Gethsemane, and *said to His disciples, “Sit here while I go over there and pray.” And He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, and began to be grieved and distressed. Then He *said to them, “My soul is deeply grieved, to the point of death; remain here and keep watch with Me.”

lines.text: Gethsemane means 'oil press'; a commentator the video cites places it in an olive grove on the western slope of the Mount of Olives.
When many would want people around them, Jesus goes to be alone with the Father. No one else has taken on the sins of the whole world in death.

SOUL.title: Why are you in despair, O my soul?

left.text: Why are you in despair, O my soul? / And why are you disturbed within me? / Wait for God, for I shall still praise Him, / For the salvation of His presence.

right.text: Then I will go to the altar of God, / To God my exceeding joy; / And upon the lyre I shall praise You, O God, my God.

lines.text: 'Deeply grieved' recalls the three refrains of Psalms 42-43 (42:5, 11; 43:5), where despair turns to joy. The video suggests the three refrains may parallel the temple's outer court, holy place and holy of holies, drawing nearer to God's presence.
It also points to Isaiah 38:1, where Hezekiah 'became ill to the point of death.'

src.text: It is a night to be kept for Yahweh for having brought them out from the land of Egypt; this night is for Yahweh, to be kept by all the sons of Israel throughout their generations.

lines.text: 'Keep watch with Me' may be a call to observe leil shimmurim, 'the night of watching,' which Jews kept on Passover night to remember the Lord's protection in Egypt.

left.text: And He went a little beyond them, and fell on His face and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; yet not as I will, but as You will.”

right.text: Awaken yourself! Awaken yourself! Arise, O Jerusalem, / You who have drunk from the hand of Yahweh the cup of His wrath; / The chalice of reeling you have drained to the dregs.

lines.text: In the Old Testament the cup means suffering and the wrath of God; Ezekiel speaks of 'the cup of horror and desolation' (Ezekiel 23:33).
Scholars call this Jesus' human temptability: an inclination to avoid the wrath, immediately surrendered to the Father's will, three times.

src.text: “Pray, then, in this way: / ‘Our Father who is in heaven, / Hallowed be Your name. / Your kingdom come. / Your will be done, / On earth as it is in heaven.

lines.text: Jesus' prayer has three elements of the prayer He taught: an address to God as Father, a request for deliverance, and submission to His will. 'Keep watching and praying that you may not enter into temptation' matches 'do not lead us into temptation' (6:13).
Both Jesus and the disciples face temptation; where they fail, He succeeds. They let their guard down.

left.text: Be of sober spirit, be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.

right.text: praying at all times with all prayer and petition in the Spirit, and to this end, being on the alert with all perseverance and petition for all the saints,

lines.text: The disciples went on to give the same warning. Paul adds that God 'will provide the way of escape also' (1 Corinthians 10:13); Jesus shows that the way of escape centers on prayer.

BACKGROUND.p: Olive groves covered the Mount of Olives, and presses crushed the olives for oil. The traditional site lies across the Kidron Valley from the temple, beside today's Church of All Nations.
The Passover meal ran late into the night, and Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. Jesus' group would have walked down through the Kidron Valley to reach the Mount of Olives.
Praying the same prayer repeatedly was familiar in Israel; Daniel prayed three times a day (Daniel 6:10), and Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:8).

DEBATES.p: Most read the cup as God's wrath against sin, borne by Jesus. Others stress suffering and death in general. The previous episode noted a reading tied to the fourth Passover cup.
The prayer 'not as I will, but as You will' led the early church to affirm that Christ has a human will fully submitted to the divine (Third Council of Constantinople, 681).
The video links the three refrains of Psalms 42-43 to the temple's three areas. This is a suggestion; the psalms do not say it.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: Luke's parallel to the warning is Luke 22:31-38, not Luke 21.
Isaiah 38:1 shares the phrase 'to the point of death' (Hezekiah's illness); the closer echo of 'deeply grieved' is the refrain of Psalms 42-43.
The quotation 'We tend to use prayer as a last resort...' is attributed to Oswald Chambers; the source was not checked here.
The temple had more than three areas (courts of the Gentiles, women and Israel, the holy place and the holy of holies); 'three levels' is a simplification.

QUESTIONS: Why do you think all the disciples, not only Peter, vowed to die with Jesus?
What do Psalms 42-43 add to 'My soul is deeply grieved'?
How does Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane follow the Lord's Prayer?
Where in your life is 'the spirit willing, but the flesh weak'?
Is prayer your first line of defense or your last resort?
What one change would make your prayer more persistent and intentional?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: the victory of the Christian in moments of testing and temptation trades on persistent, intentional prayer to their heavenly Father. The disciples' words wrote checks their bodies could not cash. The flesh will fail; where the flesh fails, prayer succeeds. The teacher tells of being stuck in a hotel during a 2023 ice storm and being convicted that he prayed only after trying everything else; since then, he says, his prayer life has never been the same.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): pray the Lord's Prayer slowly each morning this week, pausing at 'Your will be done' and 'do not lead us into temptation' to name your specific situation.

   (video) 'Fall away' is a form of skandalizō, the word of Jesus' warning to John's disciples: 'blessed is he who does not take offense at Me' (11:6). The disciples will do the very thing He warned against. (Matthew 11:6)
   (video) Jesus speaks of 'after I have been raised' (26:32); in John He says He will raise up the sanctuary of His body (John 2:19-21; 10:18). Both descriptions of the resurrection stand. (John 2:19-21; John 10:18)
2. Matthew 26:33-35: 'I will never fall away'
   All said the same Matthew 26:34-35: "Jesus said to him, “Truly I say to you that this very night, before a rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.” Peter *said to Him, “Even if I have to die with You, I will not deny You.” All the disciples said the same thing too." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+26:34-35

## Key people
- Peter: Vows never to fall away and to die with Jesus. [Background] Luke adds that Jesus prayed for Peter's faith (Luke 22:32).
- The two sons of Zebedee: James and John, taken with Peter deeper into the garden. [Background] They had said they could drink His cup (20:22).
- The disciples: All vow to die with Him; all fall asleep. [Background] 'Their eyes were heavy' (26:43).
- Hezekiah: Ill 'to the point of death' in Isaiah 38:1. [Background] King of Judah who prayed and was given fifteen more years (Isaiah 38:5).

- Gethsemane (traditional) (named in the video): 'A place called Gethsemane' (26:36), the oil press.

## Key terms
- Gethsemane: 'Oil press': an olive grove at the Mount of Olives.
- Skandalizō: To cause to stumble or fall away; to take offense.
- Leil shimmurim: 'Night of watching': Passover night kept for the Lord (Exodus 12:42).
- The cup: An Old Testament image of suffering and of God's wrath.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Gethsemane: Olive groves covered the Mount of Olives, and presses crushed the olives for oil. The traditional site lies across the Kidron Valley from the temple, beside today's Church of All Nations.
- Passover night: The Passover meal ran late into the night, and Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. Jesus' group would have walked down through the Kidron Valley to reach the Mount of Olives.
- Praying three times: Praying the same prayer repeatedly was familiar in Israel; Daniel prayed three times a day (Daniel 6:10), and Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed (2 Corinthians 12:8).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- What was the cup? Most read the cup as God's wrath against sin, borne by Jesus. Others stress suffering and death in general. The previous episode noted a reading tied to the fourth Passover cup.
- Jesus' human will The prayer 'not as I will, but as You will' led the early church to affirm that Christ has a human will fully submitted to the divine (Third Council of Constantinople, 681).
- Three refrains, three courts? The video links the three refrains of Psalms 42-43 to the temple's three areas. This is a suggestion; the psalms do not say it.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- Luke's parallel to the warning is Luke 22:31-38, not Luke 21.
- Isaiah 38:1 shares the phrase 'to the point of death' (Hezekiah's illness); the closer echo of 'deeply grieved' is the refrain of Psalms 42-43.
- The quotation 'We tend to use prayer as a last resort...' is attributed to Oswald Chambers; the source was not checked here.
- The temple had more than three areas (courts of the Gentiles, women and Israel, the holy place and the holy of holies); 'three levels' is a simplification.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why do you think all the disciples, not only Peter, vowed to die with Jesus?
2. What do Psalms 42-43 add to 'My soul is deeply grieved'?
3. How does Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane follow the Lord's Prayer?
4. Where in your life is 'the spirit willing, but the flesh weak'?
5. Is prayer your first line of defense or your last resort?
6. What one change would make your prayer more persistent and intentional?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: the victory of the Christian in moments of testing and temptation trades on persistent, intentional prayer to their heavenly Father. The disciples' words wrote checks their bodies could not cash. The flesh will fail; where the flesh fails, prayer succeeds. The teacher tells of being stuck in a hotel during a 2023 ice storm and being convicted that he prayed only after trying everything else; since then, he says, his prayer life has never been the same.
- Study note (added): pray the Lord's Prayer slowly each morning this week, pausing at 'Your will be done' and 'do not lead us into temptation' to name your specific situation.
